body:
The Meaning of Remote Sensing

Remote sensing is the acquisition of information about an object, area or phenomenon without making direct physical contact with it. Satellite remote sensing measures electromagnetic radiation associated with the Earth's surface or atmosphere and uses those measurements to infer conditions on the ground.

A satellite image is not simply a photograph taken from very far away. Its sensors may record information at wavelengths invisible to the human eye. Scientists analyse these measurements to identify vegetation, water, built-up areas, soil conditions, cloud patterns and changes over time.

Satellite observations are useful because they can cover large areas repeatedly. A single field visit gives detailed information at one location, whereas repeated satellite observations help compare many locations or follow changes through a season.

Passive and Active Remote Sensing

Passive sensors detect naturally available electromagnetic radiation. In visible and near-infrared observations, much of this radiation is sunlight reflected by the Earth's surface. Thermal sensors measure radiation emitted by objects because of their temperature.

Active sensors transmit their own signal and record the energy returned from the target. Radar is an important example. Radar satellites transmit microwave signals and measure the returned signal to obtain information about surface conditions.

FeatureOptical remote sensingRadar remote sensing
SignalUsually reflected sunlightMicrowaves transmitted by the sensor
Operation at nightReflected-sunlight imaging is limitedCan operate at night
CloudsThick clouds obstruct surface observationsCan observe through most cloud cover
Common usesVegetation, visible land features and water mappingFlood mapping, surface change and soil-moisture studies

Radar is not completely unaffected by atmospheric conditions or the nature of the ground. Its return also depends on surface roughness, moisture and vegetation. Optical and radar measurements therefore complement each other rather than providing identical information.

Understanding Satellite Image Resolution

A satellite observation must be judged by the type of detail it can provide.

  • Spatial resolution: The size of the ground area represented by an image pixel. Smaller pixels can show finer features.
  • Temporal resolution: How frequently a satellite or satellite system can observe the same location.
  • Spectral resolution: The ability to distinguish small differences in wavelength; narrower wavelength bands provide finer spectral resolution.
  • Radiometric resolution: The ability to distinguish differences in the intensity of the detected radiation.

A high-detail image is not automatically updated more frequently. A sensor that revisits an area frequently does not automatically provide the finest spatial detail. The correct satellite data must be selected according to the task.

From Image to Thematic Map

A thematic map presents information about one subject, such as forests, crops, rainfall, settlements or water bodies. Its purpose differs from a general map showing roads and administrative boundaries.

To prepare a useful thematic map, the satellite observations are interpreted and classified. A map showing cultivated land may identify where crops are growing, while a map showing urban expansion may identify new built-up areas. Ground observations help verify whether the classifications are correct.

A Geographic Information System (GIS) stores, combines, analyses and displays information linked to geographical locations. For example, a GIS can combine a satellite-derived flood boundary with roads, villages, schools and hospitals. This makes it possible to identify which facilities may be affected.

Geospatial data means information with a location component. Georeferencing means placing information into a geographical coordinate system so it can be compared with other maps. Ground truth refers to observations or measurements obtained on the ground to check satellite-based interpretations.

Bhuvan and National Geospatial Data

Bhuvan is an Indian geospatial platform associated with NRSC, ISRO. It provides access to satellite imagery, thematic layers and applications for resource monitoring, planning and disaster management.

Users may examine different information layers, but these layers have different scales, data periods and purposes. A satellite-based land-cover map is not automatically a legally authoritative property-boundary record. Decisions involving ownership or exact survey boundaries require the relevant official land records and appropriate survey procedures.

NISAR: A Major Radar Mission

NISAR stands for NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar. It is a joint mission of ISRO and the United States' National Aeronautics and Space Administration. NISAR was launched by GSLV-F16 on 30 July 2025.

It carries complementary radar systems: an L-band radar supplied by NASA and an S-band radar supplied by ISRO. Their observations help study surface changes, agricultural activity, forests, soil moisture, mangroves and ground deformation.

Status at 4 November 2026: ISRO's 24 July 2026 announcement described NISAR as being in its science-operations phase and releasing S-band data products. ISRO and NASA's 17 August 2026 update also reported continuing observations and scientific applications. Its importance for preliminary examinations lies in its joint ownership, radar-based Earth observation and ability to obtain measurements through cloud cover and at night.

Prelims focus

  • Remote sensing acquires information without direct physical contact.
  • Passive optical sensing uses naturally available radiation; active radar transmits its own signal.
  • Spatial resolution and temporal resolution describe different properties.
  • GIS combines geographically referenced information for analysis.
  • Bhuvan is associated with NRSC, ISRO.
  • Trap: Satellite imagery is not automatically an authoritative cadastral or ownership record.

[NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, chapter 4, Maps, pp. 24-27, 2018-19 reprint; ISRO, NISAR S-Band SAR Data Products Release, 24 July 2026; ISRO, ISRO and NASA Celebrate One Successful Year of NISAR Mission on Orbit, 17 August 2026; NRSC, Bhuvan Services and Thematic Data Products; BISAG-N, About Us, Remote Sensing Applications and Geo-informatics sections; consulted 4 November 2026.]

title: Remote Sensing, Satellite Images and Geographic Information Systems

body:
Why Agriculture Requires Repeated Observations

Agriculture changes through the year. Fields are prepared, seeds are sown, crops grow, irrigation is applied and crops are harvested. Satellite observations taken at different stages can help identify cultivated areas and changes in crop condition.

For Gujarat, important examples include cotton, groundnut and wheat. Cropping patterns differ between the rain-fed agricultural areas of Saurashtra and areas with greater irrigation access. A satellite-based agricultural assessment must therefore consider the crop season, irrigation, rainfall and regional conditions.

The kharif season is associated mainly with the monsoon, while rabi crops are generally grown in the cooler post-monsoon period. A field that appears bare in one season may be cultivated in another. Consequently, an image showing no crop at one moment does not prove that the land is permanently unused.

How Satellites Detect Vegetation

Healthy green vegetation absorbs much of the visible red light used in photosynthesis and reflects substantial near-infrared radiation. Sensors that measure these wavelength bands can help distinguish vegetation from bare soil and many other surfaces.

A false-colour composite displays selected measured bands as visible colours. In a common near-infrared composite, healthy vegetation appears bright red. That red appearance is an image-display convention, not the crop's actual colour.

Vegetation indices, including the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), summarise differences in reflected radiation that are useful for assessing vegetation cover and condition. A low vegetation-index value may reflect sparse growth, but it must be interpreted carefully. Bare soil, recently harvested fields, seasonal growth and crop stress can produce different appearances.

Satellite observations alone do not directly reveal the exact harvest weight of every field. Reliable crop-production estimates combine remote-sensing information with weather observations, crop models, field surveys and other agricultural data.

Crop Acreage, Condition and Production Estimates

Crop acreage estimation identifies the area under a particular crop. Crop-condition monitoring examines how vegetation develops. Yield estimation concerns production per unit area, whereas production estimation concerns the total crop output.

These quantities are connected but distinct. A large cultivated area does not guarantee a large harvest if drought, disease or other adverse conditions reduce yield.

Major Indian Agricultural Remote-Sensing Programmes

FASAL

FASAL stands for Forecasting Agricultural Output using Space, Agro-meteorology and Land-based Observations. It combines satellite observations, weather-related information and ground-based data to prepare agricultural production forecasts.

The Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre (MNCFC), under the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, performs an operational role in national crop forecasting. The Space Applications Centre, Ahmedabad, develops remote-sensing methodologies, while NRSC, Hyderabad, supplies relevant satellite data. The India Meteorological Department provides weather-related inputs.

This demonstrates a major Gujarat connection: SAC in Ahmedabad contributes to an agricultural forecasting system used at the national level.

NADAMS

NADAMS means National Agricultural Drought Assessment and Monitoring System. It combines information on vegetation condition, rainfall and other relevant indicators to assess agricultural drought. ISRO and agricultural agencies developed the system, and operational use was transferred to MNCFC.

Agricultural drought is not identical to meteorological drought. A prolonged rainfall deficiency is a meteorological condition; agricultural drought concerns inadequate moisture for crop growth. Rainfall, soil moisture, the crop's stage of growth and irrigation availability can affect agricultural conditions differently.

CHAMAN

CHAMAN stands for Coordinated Horticulture Assessment and Management using Geoinformatics. It applies geospatial methods to horticultural assessment. Horticulture includes activities involving fruits, vegetables and other horticultural crops, and its mapping needs can differ from those of extensive field crops.

Space Inputs for Crop Insurance

The Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) is India's crop-insurance scheme. Satellite observations may support crop mapping, selection of field-sampling locations and yield-estimation systems used in insurance assessment.

Under the YES-TECH initiative, technology-based methods are used to support yield estimation. ISRO's contributions include geospatial techniques and improved sampling methods. However, crop-insurance assessment follows the applicable scheme rules and procedures. A satellite image does not automatically establish a payable insurance claim.

In a statement issued on 18 March 2026, the Government of India identified FASAL, NADAMS and CHAMAN among the principal space-based initiatives supporting agriculture. These are programme names rather than names of individual satellites.

Practical Use in Gujarat

Suppose a district experiences poor monsoon rainfall. Repeated satellite observations can show whether crop vegetation is developing normally or remaining sparse. Rainfall and soil-moisture information help distinguish a possible moisture problem from a field that has not yet been sown. Administrative and field data then help officials assess conditions and plan a response.

Remote sensing is valuable because it provides comparable information across many villages. Its conclusions become more reliable when local cropping calendars, irrigation sources and field observations are included.

Prelims focus

  • Near-infrared information helps distinguish vegetation from many other surfaces.
  • Healthy vegetation commonly appears red in a standard near-infrared false-colour composite.
  • FASAL: agricultural forecasting using space, agrometeorological and ground observations.
  • MNCFC: national operational crop-forecasting institution under the agriculture ministry.
  • NADAMS: agricultural drought assessment; CHAMAN: horticultural geospatial assessment.
  • Trap: Crop area, yield and total production are different quantities.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, chapter 1, Crop Production and Management, pp. 1-6, 2018-19 reprint; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, chapter 5, Land Resources and Agriculture, pp. 40-44; ISRO, Agriculture and Soil, crop forecasting and FASAL sections; Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, FASAL, component-wise scheme details; Press Information Bureau, Parliament Question: Space-Based Initiatives for Agriculture, 18 March 2026; NRSC, Disaster Management Support, Agricultural Drought section; consulted 4 November 2026.]
